lead: A link must carry a signal far enough and fast enough. Loss sets how far: every kilometre removes power, and the receiver needs a minimum. Rise time sets how fast: a pulse that spreads too much overlaps its neighbour. This chapter builds the rise-time budget, turns it into a maximum length from dispersion, compares that length with the attenuation limit, and shows that the shorter of the two is the real reach. It is used in choosing fiber, source and receiver for a new route.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for PT, PR and margin M; Unit 2 for chromatic and modal dispersion.

blocks.text: Every digital link has a clock. The bit period T<sub>b</sub> is the time allowed for one bit. If the bit rate is B bit/s, then T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B. At 1 Gbit/s, T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ns = 1000 ps. At 10 Gbit/s it is 100 ps. A pulse must rise and fall inside this slot. Its 10% to 90% rise time is T<sub>r</sub>. If T<sub>r</sub> is too large, the pulse smears into the next slot and the receiver cannot decide between 0 and 1. This overlap is inter-symbol interference, ISI.

A non-return-to-zero (NRZ) pulse stays high for the whole bit slot. A return-to-zero (RZ) pulse is high for part of the slot and returns to zero, so it needs a faster transition. The usual rule is: the system rise time T<sub>sys</sub> must be at most 0.7T<sub>b</sub> for NRZ and 0.35T<sub>b</sub> for RZ. The 0.7 factor lets the received pulse fill most of the slot without touching its neighbour. Some syllabi call the same check the bandwidth budget.
T<sub>sys</sub> = √(T<sub>tx</sub>² + T<sub>fiber</sub>² + T<sub>rx</sub>²) ≤ 0.7 T<sub>b</sub> for NRZ, and ≤ 0.35 T<sub>b</sub> for RZ
blocks.where: T<sub>sys</sub> is the total system rise time (10–90%) in ps; T<sub>tx</sub>, T<sub>fiber</sub> and T<sub>rx</sub> are the transmitter, fiber and receiver rise times in ps; T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B is the bit period in ps; B is the bit rate in bit/s.

blocks.text: T<sub>sys</sub> is not the sum of the parts. Three independent broadenings add as squares: transmitter T<sub>tx</sub>, fiber T<sub>fiber</sub>, receiver T<sub>rx</sub>. This square-root rule comes from adding variances of independent Gaussian-like responses. It is why a fast receiver cannot fully cure a slow fiber. Each term must be a 10–90% rise time in the same unit, usually picoseconds.

T<sub>fiber</sub> has two possible sources. In multimode fiber, different modes travel different paths and arrive at different times. That is modal dispersion, covered in Unit 2. In single-mode fiber there is only one mode, but different wavelengths travel at different speeds. That is chromatic dispersion. A source is never perfectly monochromatic. Its spectral width Δλ is the spread of wavelengths. Use the root-mean-square (RMS) width, not the full width at half maximum, unless the data sheet says otherwise.

blocks.where: T<sub>chrom</sub> is the chromatic rise time in ps; D is the dispersion coefficient in ps/(nm·km); L is fiber length in km; Δλ is the RMS source spectral width in nm. The absolute value handles negative D.

blocks.text: If L = 20 km, D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and Δλ = 2 nm, then T<sub>chrom</sub> = 17 × 20 × 2 = 680 ps. A laser with Δλ = 0.1 nm would give 34 ps, twenty times smaller. That is why narrow-linewidth lasers matter at high bit rates.

If a fiber has both modal and chromatic broadening, combine them in quadrature: T<sub>fiber</sub> = √(T<sub>modal</sub>² + T<sub>chrom</sub>²). In pure single-mode fiber T<sub>modal</sub> is zero. Polarization-mode dispersion also broadens pulses, but its statistical nature is treated separately.

The attenuation limit asks how long the fiber can be before received power falls below sensitivity. Rearrange the power budget of 5.2: Latt = (PT − PR − M)/α. PT is launched power in dBm, PR is receiver sensitivity in dBm, M is system margin in dB, and α is fiber attenuation in dB/km. The numerator is in dB, so Latt is in km. If PT = 0 dBm, PR = −28 dBm, M = 0 dB and α = 0.22 dB/km, then Latt = 28/0.22 = 127 km. Connectors, splices and ageing margin must already be inside M or subtracted separately.

The dispersion limit asks how far a pulse can travel before its spread reaches one bit slot. A simple criterion is B L |D| Δλ ≤ 1. Here B is bit rate in bit/s, D is in s/(nm·km) when using SI units, and Δλ is in nm. Solving gives L<sub>disp</sub> = 1/(B D Δλ). With B in Gbit/s and D in ps/(nm·km), multiply by 1000: L<sub>disp</sub> = 1000/(B<sub>Gb</sub> D<sub>ps</sub> Δλ). The figure uses D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and Δλ = 0.1 nm, so L<sub>disp</sub> = 588/B<sub>Gb</sub> km: 588 km at 1 Gbit/s and 58.8 km at 10 Gbit/s. A 100 km loss limit crosses this near 5.9 Gbit/s.

The real reach is the smaller of L<sub>att</sub> and L<sub>disp</sub>. At low bit rates loss usually wins; at high bit rates dispersion wins. If the reach is too short, first reduce Δλ or use a lower-dispersion fiber, then increase power or sensitivity. The rise-time budget is stricter than the simple dispersion limit because it includes transmitter and receiver rise times and the 0.7 factor. The dispersion limit is a quick first estimate.

figure.caption: Maximum length against bit rate. The flat line is the loss limit; the falling curve is the dispersion limit, and the smaller value sets the reach.

spec.aria: Plot of maximum link length against bit rate: a flat line at 100 km for the attenuation limit and a falling curve for the dispersion limit, crossing near 5.9 Gb/s.

examples.question: A 1 Gbit/s NRZ link uses 20 km of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm. The transmitter rise time is 250 ps, the receiver rise time is 350 ps, the source RMS spectral width is 2 nm, and the fiber dispersion is D = 17 ps/(nm·km). The launched power is 0 dBm, receiver sensitivity is −28 dBm, margin is 0 dB, and attenuation is 0.22 dB/km. Does the link pass the rise-time budget? If not, what is the maximum fiber length allowed by the rise-time budget? Check whether loss is the limiting factor.
steps: Bit period: T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B = 1/(1 × 10<sup>9</sup>) s = 1 ns = 1000 ps.
Allowed system rise time for NRZ: 0.7T<sub>b</sub> = 0.7 × 1000 = 700 ps.
Actual chromatic rise time: T<sub>chrom</sub> = |D|LΔλ = 17 × 20 × 2 = 680 ps.
Compare: 680 ps > 552.3 ps, so the link fails the rise-time budget.
Maximum length from rise time: L = 552.3/(17 × 2) = 16.2 km.
Loss check: fiber loss = 20 × 0.22 = 4.4 dB. Available budget = P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> − M = 0 − (−28) − 0 = 28 dB. Since 4.4 dB < 28 dB, loss passes easily.
examples.answer: The link fails the rise-time budget; the maximum length is 16.2 km, while the loss check needs only 4.4 dB of the 28 dB available, so rise time sets the reach.
examples.check:
import math
B = 1e9
Tb = 1/B * 1e12
allow = 0.7 * Tb
Tf = math.sqrt(allow**2 - 250**2 - 350**2)
actual = 17 * 2 * 20
Lmax = Tf / (17 * 2)
loss = 20 * 0.22
avail = 0 - (-28) - 0
print(round(Tb, 1))
print(round(allow, 1))
print(round(Tf, 1))
print(round(actual, 1))
print(round(Lmax, 1))
print(round(loss, 1))
print(round(avail, 1))

traps: Adding T<sub>tx</sub>, T<sub>fiber</sub> and T<sub>rx</sub> directly. They add in quadrature, not as a plain sum.
Using the full spectral width instead of the RMS width in T<sub>chrom</sub> = |D|LΔλ.
Mixing ps and ns: T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B gives seconds; multiply by 10<sup>12</sup> for ps.
Forgetting to compare L<sub>disp</sub> with L<sub>att</sub>. The reach is the smaller, not the dispersion limit alone.

quiz.q: Write the rise-time budget condition for an NRZ link.
Why are rise times added in quadrature and not directly?
quiz.a: Independent broadening mechanisms add as variances, so their standard deviations add as squares; direct addition would overestimate the total.

quiz.q: A 2.5 Gbit/s NRZ link has T<sub>tx</sub> = 100 ps, T<sub>rx</sub> = 200 ps and T<sub>fiber</sub> = 400 ps. Does it pass?
quiz.a: T<sub>b</sub> = 400 ps, allowed = 280 ps. T<sub>sys</sub> = √(100² + 400² + 200²) = √210000 = 458.3 ps > 280 ps, so it fails.

quiz.q: Find L<sub>disp</sub> at 10 Gbit/s for D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and Δλ = 0.1 nm.
A link has L<sub>att</sub> = 80 km and L<sub>disp</sub> = 120 km at 2 Gbit/s. What is the reach? What happens at 4 Gbit/s?
quiz.a: Reach is 80 km. At 4 Gbit/s, L<sub>disp</sub> halves to 60 km, so dispersion becomes the limit and reach falls to 60 km.

quiz.q: What does the 0.7 factor in the NRZ rise-time budget allow?
quiz.a: It lets the received pulse occupy most of the bit slot while leaving margin against overlap with the next pulse.

quiz.q: Why can a link pass the power budget but fail the rise-time budget?
quiz.a: Loss may be small, but pulse spreading from limited source linewidth or long fiber can exceed the allowed rise time and cause ISI.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real links now use coherent receivers and digital signal processing, so chromatic dispersion is compensated electronically after detection rather than only by choosing fiber. Flexgrid and high-order modulation make the bandwidth budget a filter-design problem, not just a rise-time sum. Search next for coherent optical OFDM, digital backpropagation, and dispersion compensation in DSP.
